questions.question: A company runs WordPress on an Auto Scaling group spread across three Availability Zones behind a load balancer. Users report that images uploaded moments ago sometimes appear as broken images, and the problem gets worse as more instances launch. The database is unaffected. What is the most likely cause?
options: Images are stored on an EBS volume attached to each instance, so other instances cannot see them
Images are stored in Amazon EFS but the mount targets are only in one Availability Zone
The Multi-AZ RDS standby is not being used to serve image reads
The load balancer is not sticky enough to route each user to the instance holding their upload
questions.explanation: EBS is block storage attached to a single instance in a single AZ, so an upload written on one instance is invisible to the others in the Auto Scaling group. EFS would be visible to all instances, so it is not the cause; the RDS standby is for failover and never serves image reads; stickiness would not help because new instances still lack previously uploaded files.

questions.question: Which statement best describes the difference between Amazon EBS and Amazon EFS in the context of uploaded images in a distributed application?
options: EBS is a shared file system; EFS is block storage attached to one instance
EBS is block storage attached to one instance; EFS is a file system many instances can mount
Both are AZ-scoped block volumes, but EFS allows multi-attach across AZs
Both are Regional file systems, but EBS has lower latency for uploads
questions.explanation: EBS provides block storage attached to a single instance, while EFS is a shared network file system mountable by many instances. The reversed option swaps the two; EFS is not block storage and can be mounted across AZs; and EBS is not Regional nor a file system.
questions.keyTopic: EBS vs EFS for distributed apps

questions.question: A WordPress site runs on EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group across Availability Zones 1, 2 and 3, and user uploads must be readable by any instance. How should the images be stored?
options: On an EBS volume in Availability Zone 1 and shared with the other zones
On an EBS volume attached to each instance, synchronized between instances
On Amazon EFS, mounted by every instance in the Auto Scaling group
On the root EBS volume of the instance that receives the upload
questions.explanation: EFS is the shared file system all instances across AZs can mount, so any instance can serve any upload. EBS volumes cannot be shared across Availability Zones; per-instance EBS with synchronization is not the section's design and does not provide shared storage; and a root volume is likewise single-instance.

questions.question: How do EC2 instances in different Availability Zones mount the same Amazon EFS file system?
options: Each instance mounts it through an elastic network interface (ENI) in its own Availability Zone
Only the instance in Availability Zone 1 mounts it and the others copy the files over EBS
Instances attach the same EBS volume to reach the EFS mount point
All instances must be launched in a single Availability Zone to use one EFS file system
questions.explanation: In the section's design every instance mounts EFS via an ENI located in its own Availability Zone, giving all instances one shared file system. EFS does not rely on a single mounting instance or on EBS volumes, and it does not require all instances to be in one AZ.

questions.question: A single EC2 instance runs a small internal WordPress site with no Auto Scaling and stores uploaded images locally. What is the appropriate storage choice for those images?
options: Amazon EFS, because file storage is always preferred over block storage
Amazon EBS, because the application is single-instance
Amazon Aurora Read Replicas, because they offload image reads
An EBS volume replicated across three Availability Zones
questions.explanation: The EBS single-instance limitation only matters once instances span AZs, so for a genuinely single-instance application an EBS volume is acceptable. EFS is unnecessary here; Read Replicas scale database reads and hold no image files; and a single EBS volume exists in one Availability Zone.

questions.question: A WordPress deployment uses RDS MySQL Multi-AZ for user data and blog content. The team notices high read traffic on the database and asks whether the Multi-AZ standby can absorb it. What is the correct assessment?
options: Yes — the Multi-AZ standby serves read traffic, so no other change is needed
No — the Multi-AZ standby is for failover; read scaling needs Read Replicas or Aurora Read Replicas
Yes — but only if the standby is promoted first, which doubles cost
No — Multi-AZ must be disabled before any read traffic can be scaled
questions.explanation: In RDS Multi-AZ the standby exists for failover / high availability, not read scaling. The standby does not serve reads; promotion is a failover action, not a scaling mechanism; and disabling Multi-AZ reduces availability rather than enabling read scaling.

questions.question: A database layer must both survive an Availability Zone failure and handle a read-heavy WordPress workload with the least operational effort. Which design does this section recommend?
options: A single RDS MySQL instance with snapshots taken every hour
RDS MySQL Multi-AZ only, relying on the standby for read traffic
Amazon Aurora MySQL Multi-AZ with Read Replicas
Amazon EFS mounted by the database instances to share read load
questions.explanation: Aurora provides easy Multi-AZ high availability and Read Replicas for read scaling, matching both requirements with minimal management. A single instance with snapshots is not highly available; RDS Multi-AZ alone gives failover but no read scaling; and EFS is file storage for uploaded images, not a database read-scaling mechanism.

questions.question: A team proposes attaching the same EBS volume to every instance of a multi-AZ Auto Scaling group so all instances can read uploaded images. Why does this fail to meet the requirement?
options: EBS volumes can be attached to only one instance at a time and exist in a single Availability Zone
EBS volumes cannot store image files, only database files
EBS volumes are Regional and too slow for uploads from multiple AZs
EBS volumes require an EFS mount point before they can be attached
questions.explanation: An EBS volume is AZ-scoped and attached to one instance, so it cannot be shared by instances in different Availability Zones — that is the EFS pattern. EBS can store any files including images; it is not Regional; and attaching an EFS mount point to an EBS volume is not a real configuration.
